wires/fc: A linear classifier has a weight for every pair of input and output. Draw each weight as a line, and every input is wired to every output: seven inputs and five outputs make thirty five lines.
wires/name: A layer like that is called fully connected, because nothing is left unconnected. Add one bias per output, and it learns forty numbers.
wires/conv: A convolution wires each output only to the patch under its filter: three lines each, fifteen in all.
wires/share: And every patch uses the same three weights. Color each line by its weight, and only three colors appear: fifteen lines, but three weights to learn.
wires/sharing: That is weight sharing: one small filter, reused at every position. With its one bias, it is four numbers, however long the row.
wires/lecun: In 1989, Yann LeCun and colleagues at Bell Labs built this into a reader for handwritten zip codes. It had over sixty four thousand connections, lines like these, but fewer than ten thousand numbers to learn.
wires/belief: Their reason: the kinds of patterns that matter in one place of an image are likely to matter in other places too.
count/layer: Now a real layer on a color image: n n dot conv two d, of three, eight and three. Three channels in, eight filters, each three by three.
count/F: Call the side of a filter F: here, three.
count/C: Each filter reaches through every channel of its input, C of them, here red, green and blue. So it holds F by F weights, three times over: twenty seven.
count/bias: Plus one bias, added after the sum, just as in a linear classifier: twenty eight numbers per filter.
count/K: The layer has K filters, each with its own weights and bias. Eight of them: eight times twenty eight, two hundred and twenty four.
count/formula: So a layer learns K, times F times F times C, plus one.
count/dials: Double K, and the count exactly doubles. Double C, and the weights double but the biases do not: a little under double. Double F, and every F by F square holds four times as many weights.
size/missing: Notice what the count leaves out: the size of the image. The same two hundred and twenty four numbers slide over every position, so a bigger image means more work, but not one more parameter.
size/sizes: Now a fully connected layer from the same image to the same output. The image, three by thirty two by thirty two, holds three thousand and seventy two numbers. The output, eight by thirty by thirty, holds seven thousand two hundred.
size/fc: A weight for every pair, plus a bias per output: over twenty two million parameters, against two hundred and twenty four.
size/why: Sharing one small filter is what makes convolution cheap, and it builds in that belief: a pattern worth finding in one place is worth finding everywhere.
